utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the appearances for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence. And I think that our phones are not working, headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Maybe we could have some technician to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's working now. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I haven't heard, for the Defence, appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, Judge Schomburg is still ill. For the same reasons as stated previously, considering that Dr. Trifkovic is still in The Hague and has not yet concluded his testimony, it is in the interest of justice for Judge Argibay and I to continue sitting under Rule 15 bis to hear him. For the record, I would again ask both parties and Dr. Stakic himself formally register their consent to this procedure for today's hearing, 14th March, year 2003. Starting with the Prosecution, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We consent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, considering that Judge Schomburg is still ill and not available to sit in this case today, Judge Argibay and I being satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so, and again based on the consent of the parties and Dr. Stakic himself hereby order pursuant to the Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that the hearing continue in the absence of Judge Schomburg. Before I call the witness into the courtroom, could I ask the Defence if there are any updates and breaking news in relation to the witnesses that will be available to testify next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's news, but not breaking news. We will not be able to bring Witness 058 to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Will not be able.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will not be able.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about Witness 089?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the situation is the same, so we will not be able to bring this witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about the Father Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Ostojic is in charge of this witness, and for now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But the Defence is one team as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is really, and we think that we work as one team. But I think that this witness will not be able to testify in front of this Tribunal live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for your information. Could the usher please --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before, sorry, just before you bring the witness in, Your Honour, may I know whether it is apparent that the witness cannot finish today, may I know whether the witness will be ordered to return on Monday or at a later stage? Because that will make a difference as to how I conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Well only for you, Ms. Korner, we decided to ask the witness to stay on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful to Your Honours indeed. The consideration shown by this Trial Chamber is touching, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still under the solemn declaration. I think the parties and the witness himself have been given notice of our ruling in relation of your stay in The Hague. I will now read the Court's written order in this regard dated today, 14th March, year 2003, which was filed earlier this afternoon. "Trial Chamber II of the International Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 [Tribunal], "Noting that Dr. Trifkovic, the expert historian for the Defence, started his testimony in this case on 13 March, 2003, "Noting that although the Defence had originally estimated that it would need only one hour for its direct examination of Dr. Trifkovic, it was not able to conclude the examination-in-chief of this witness yesterday in the hour and eleven minutes of the session remaining, "Noting that the Office of the Prosecutor estimated that it would need two hours to cross-examine Dr. Trifkovic, "Noting that the Chamber took the necessary steps to have the maximum possible sitting time, that is, two hours, available for today despite the fact that no hearing had been scheduled for today in this case in order based on the original estimates to be able to conclude the testimony of Dr. Trifkovic today, "Noting that the Defence now estimates that it will need more than one additional hour today to conclude the examination-in-chief of this witness, "Noting that based on the amended estimate for the length of the direct examination, it will not be possible to conclude the testimony of Dr. Trifkovic, "Noting that for administrative reasons [Courtroom availability, interpretation facilities, et cetera] it is not possible to have additional time for a hearing either today, 14 March 2003, or tomorrow, Saturday, 15 March, 2003, "Considering that it is mandatory to continue with the uninterrupted hearing of this witness in the interests of justice and, especially in the interest of granting the accused a fair trial by not imposing a time limit on the Defence for the examination-in-chief of its expert, "Considering the interests of Dr. Trifkovic and his explanation of his schedule for the next week, that is, 17 to 21 March, year 2003, "Concludes that balancing this interest, priority must be given to the interests of justice and the interests of the accused, not forgetting the fiscal interests of the international community, "Hereby orders Dr. Trifkovic to remain in The Hague until his evidence is concluded, "and emphasises that Dr. Trifkovic must bear the consequences of any breach of this order." Done in English and French, the English text being authorative. Any remarks, questions? Then let us proceed. Well, before I will give the floor to the Defence, I would like to say that in relation to the over 250 documents which Dr. Trifkovic relied upon in writing his report, the Chamber hasn't yet had an opportunity to review these documents. And as it was in the case with the Prosecution expert, Dr. Robert Donia, the Chamber is unwilling to admit them as a package. Therefore, the Chamber would suggest the Defence identify the core documents from the bundle, 250, and seek to have them admitted on an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. individual basis during Dr. Trifkovic's testimony, if it is necessary. As to the remaining documents, the Bench will rule at a later stage, at a later date. And now, the Defence. Mr. Lukic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will continue your direct examination due to the absence of my colleague, John Ostojic. And you heard that you are ordered to stay on Monday as well. We hope that it wouldn't cause too big problems for you. You know, it will be -- probably cause the inconvenience, but hopefully they will be solved. In the context of the discussion you had yesterday with Mr. Ostojic, could you be so kind and explain to us what effect if any the secession of Slovenia and Croatia had on BH, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect was three-fold. First of all, the rising level of violence in Croatia, and the apparent ineffectiveness of the YPA, both in Slovenia and Croatia, changed attitudes towards this, until that time, highly respected - and I respected from the standpoint both of people who liked the YPA and those who didn't like it, both those who feared it and who trusted it - there was a huge loss of credibility of the Yugoslav People's Army in the aftermath of the Slovene secession. It was effectively routed in Slovenia without ever trying to counter the secession. And in Croatia, in the ensuing months, displayed an inability to counter the secessionist forces, including the surrender of garrisons in for instance Bjelovar and Barusdin [phoen], with the extensive weaponry and even undamaged tanks. The second effect of the secession was to focus the minds of everybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina as to what will happen next. Izetbegovic's position was becoming increasingly clear at this time, that he would not remain in a rump Yugoslavia, and that no Yugoslavia is possible without Croatia and Slovenia, that with their departure, we are looking at a qualitatively new situation in which Bosnia-Herzegovina ought to become sovereign and independent as well. Among the Serbs, the prevalent position was that whoever wants to go is free to go, but they want to remain, and they would not be taken out of even the reduced, rump Yugoslavia, against their will. The third effect, and I don't think it can be overemphasised, is the proximity of violence on the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For as long as various political options remained in the realm of the theoretical, it was one thing. But when in August and September and October of 1991, thousands of refugees started arriving in Bosnia-Herzegovina, most notably Serbs from the urban areas of Croatia, and when the tales of horror that some of them conveyed, including the tragedy, for instance, of the Zec family in Zagreb, who I understand originally came from Prijedor, and with the engagement of the reserve units mobilised in Bosnia-Herzegovina, again notably in the border regions of Bosanska Krajina, across the River Sava and Una, all this had the effect of electrifying the public opinion and creating the sense of imminent danger and of escalating tension. So the effect, to summarise, was roughly speaking three-fold: One was the massive loss of credibility of the YPA; two, the political tension resulting from the determination of the different political forces to draw different conclusions from the secession of Slovenia and Croatia on the Croat and Muslim, the determination that they will not be left in rump Yugoslavia; on the Serbian side, not to be taken out of the Yugoslavian context. And last, but by no means least, the sense that violence is now on our doorstep, and that try as we may, we may not remain immune to it, that there was an almost relentless and fateful march of events over which the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina themselves had less and less control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, can you also help us understand when these secessions of Slovenia and Croatia happened, and why.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formal date, of course, is June 25th, 1991. But the writing had been on the wall for more than a year. Specifically with the victory of the Croatian democratic alliance, HDZ, in the spring of 1990, and the ensuing series of demands from Zagreb and Ljubljana for the reorganisation of the Yugoslav federation along the confederal principles, demands that on the Serb side were seen as only a stepping stone to full secession, because what Kucan and Tudjman were suggesting, as far as the Serbs were concerned was a de facto secession through the back door, because under the proposed confederal arrangement, the soul sovereignty would reside with the constituent republics, and they would be able at any moment through the declaration of the assembly to announce their total separation from the confederal framework. In addition, I believe that the whole concept of secessionism in the individual republics was enhanced by the piecemeal process of verifying the will of the people concerned by not having an all-Yugoslav referendum on whether people wanted to remain part of Yugoslavia or not, but by having it carried out not simultaneously, but at different times, in different republics. And in some cases, by having the referendum question itself couched in ambivalent and ambiguous language which did not imply, quite clearly, the starkness of the choice that faced the electorate. I apologise, I'm down with bronchitis, so my delivery may leave a little bit to be desired today. To this outcome, the near complete control of the media mechanism in practically all of the republics by the not ostensibly post communist ruling structures certainly made a contribution, even though in Slovenia and Croatia, which were usually branded in the western media as pro-western and reform minded, the post communist parties came to power. And in Serbia, the recycled communists led by Slobodan Milosevic reinforced their grip on power in the election of December 1990. The media climate was marked by intolerance, by black and white simplicity, and by mere demonisation of the rival ethnic groups in the presentation of the issues in a way that carried unfortunate overtones of an earlier period of 50 years earlier that were still vividly present in the collective memory of many Yugoslavs on all sides of the ethnic divide. So instead of having a comprehensive and informed debate about the choices facing them, many people in Croatia, in Serbia, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina were almost intoxicated by a heady brew of historical revisionism, and of simplified nationalist rhetoric that blurred the issues and precluded meaningful debate of the kind that, had it be carried out in the spirit of dispassionate analysis of the issues facing different people, could have contributed to the avoidance of the war. It is additionally unfortunate that the so-called voices of reason were all too often identified with the inheritance of the old communist power structure so that the most loudly Yugo nostalgist voices belonged to, for instance, the veterans' association, the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia, or federal Prime Minister Ante Markovic's reformists, all of which were in one way or another identified with the legacy of the Titoist period that was becoming thoroughly discredited and regarded as unable to provide meaningful answers and to offer a road map for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like now to move to Bosnia-Herzegovina and ask you first: Did Mr. Alija Izetbegovic get the most votes during the elections of November 1990 which resulted in him being elected president of BH pursuant to the interparty agreement reached between SDS, SDA, and HDZ. And if you can explain us what actually happened with the votes.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the actual number of votes polled, the man who is sometimes described as the maverick businessman from Velika Kladusa in the extreme northwest of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the name of Fikret Abdic was the winner. But because of the vagaries of party-political constitutional arrangements and because he didn't belong to the SDA, it was Alija Izetbegovic who was duly elected in the caucus. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Fikret Abdic undoubtedly commanded a considerable body of following among the Bosnian Muslims and was regarded as a somewhat safer bet by many when it came to the arrangements and -- with both Serbs and Croats, and when it came to the nonideological skill in finding optimal solutions, especially since his pivotal role in making the company called Agrokomerc a major player in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the accusations of financial misconduct notwithstanding, turned the Cazin area into a showcase of relative development and, again relatively speaking, prosperity in that part of the world. But in the aftermath of Izetbegovic's appointment as the president of the presidency, due as I say not to the simple number of votes polled, but to the support of the other members of the collective body, Abdic was very often regarded by the Izetbegovic establishment as a nuisance at best and a dangerous threat at worst, and ultimately proclaimed a traitor for his attempts to chart a middle road and to avoid the kind of political extremism that presented the other side with relatively little choice. It's one of those ifs that we have so many in history. We cannot answer it with any degree of certainty, whether the war could have been avoided if Abdic rather than Izetbegovic had led the Muslims. The one thing we can guess with some degree of certainty is that the outcome could not have been worse than it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, a long time before the elections in 1990, expressed his views in a book named "Islamic Declaration"?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the actual manuscript of the book antedates 1990 by quite a few years. And that it was only in 1990 that it was actually published and openly disseminated. But the opinions expressed in the book, including the view that there can be no peace and coexistence between Islamic and non-Islamic forms of social and political organisation are not particularly remarkable from the standpoint of a committed Islamist. Quite the contrary, Alija Izetbegovic's views are imminently part and parcel of the mainstream tradition of political Islam since its earliest days. And his view that the world is divided into the area of faith, the Uma, in which Islam is triumphant, and the world of war, dar al harb, in which it is yet to triumph, is eminently in line with both Koranic precepts of prophet Muhammad himself, the hadith, the traditions of the prophet, and the 14 centuries of Islamic political and military practice since the Hidra of 1622 and onwards. Let me clarify: Many people claimed that Izetbegovic's views were somehow radical, even in terms of the Islamic thought and practice. I would say that he's just a regular, run-of-the-mill Islamic fundamentalist of the kind that we encounter all over the Muslim world and that he has both the scriptural and the historical precedents for holding the beliefs that he does. Now, of course, it's an entirely different story as what the non-Muslims thought to draw as a lesson of disposition of his. But I have no doubt whatsoever in my own mind that with his beliefs and his views, such as they are, and such as they have been for the past 50-odd years, in the aftermath of September 11th, Alija Izetbegovic would not have been able to sell himself to the western world as a multiculturalist, multiethnicist, multiconfessionalist democrat. Quite the contrary, I think that one might say the Bosnian crisis in this sense came a decade too early, and provided militant Islam with a foothold in the heart of Europe, that when the first warnings of it were sounded back in the 1990s were routinely dismissed in some western quarters as paranoia or Serb propaganda. But now in the aftermath of all too many revelations about the Bosnian connection of a variety of terrorist groups and plots, and the findings of the US house of representatives task force on terrorism, that we can see in the reports by Yossef Bodansky and the James Chatres, I'm afraid that we now know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, is it common knowledge that there was presence of mujahedins in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and do you know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's an exceedingly leading question. "Is it common knowledge that there were mujahedins in.." What is the state of Dr. Trifkovic's knowledge and from what did he get that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will restate my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I thank you, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, did you have any knowledge in the past or do you have any knowledge now about the presence of the mujahedins in Bosnia-Herzegovina in early 1990s, and if you can tell us from which sources have you gathered those informations.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me emphasise that I am not aware of the active presence of militant Islamists from the rest of the Muslim world in Bosnia-Herzegovina now as we speak. But as I mentioned earlier, there's a comprehensive report by the task force of terrorism of the US House of Representatives, which unfortunately I don't have with me, but can supply the Court with subsequently. And now I'm afraid I speak from memory, which talks in some detail about a whole village in the vicinity of Travnik, formerly inhabited by the Serbs that had been taken over by the jihadists from the Arab world, Pakistan, elsewhere. Also, there had been a Bosnian connection, if you will, to various attempted or actually performed terrorist attacks, including the plan -- the attack on I believe it's Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, the planned attack on the US military bases in West Germany, and the action by the French police in the northern French city of Lille where all five of the people either apprehended or killed in the shootout at the time of a European Union top-level conference in the city, were found to have had either experience as veterans fighting for the Bosnian Muslim army or else having a Bosnian connection of some other kind. I regret not having documentation at my fingertips right now to answer your question in greater detail, but I have written on the subject, and I would be able to follow my oral testimony, once I return to the United States, with a more comprehensive written answer that would contain references to specific documents and events, dates, and names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Will you be also so kind and share with us and describe the circumstances which led to Alija Izetbegovic requesting the Bosnia-Herzegovina join an organisation of Islamic nations as a whole country.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Bosnia-Herzegovinian constitution, the president of the presidency was effectively "primus inter pares," first among equals, and was not authorised to make ad hoc decisions, especially those affecting the key political issues, including foreign relations, of the republic without reference to other members of the collective presidency, which as we know also included Serbs and Croats. But both Izetbegovic's request for the membership of the Islamic Conference Organisation on his visit to Turkey and his request for Saudi aid during a visit there on March 27th, 8th, and 9th of 1992 came as a surprise to other members of the presidency because neither the request for membership nor the request for assistance had been discussed, let alone cleared, by the collective body in advance of having been made. And of course their effect was to increase mutual mistrust and to feed the fears and the apprehensions of the non-Muslims, that Izetbegovic was not only acting unilaterally, but also that his unilateralism was strongly motivated by his Islamism and that when faced with a choice between following the dictate of his faith and its political consequences on the one hand, and the dictates of constitutionality and legality and political prudence on the other, he would opt for the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that you have a list of 65 ter exhibits somewhere in front of you. And is it true that under number 165 on that list, we have a clip from Oslobodenje, Sarajevo paper, mentioning the same event.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the article very well. I don't think I need to look at it. The other Muslim member of the Presidency, Ejup Ganic, when asked by the reporters to comment on the significance of Alija Izetbegovic's sudden departure for Saudi Arabia, declared that -- or rather, admitted that he himself was surprised and explained that the visit had a semi-private Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. character. Now, the category "semi-private visit" does not exist in the constitutional and political arrangements of Bosnia-Herzegovina of that time, and especially in as sensitive a moment as the end of March of 1992 with the Cutileiro-led negotiations entering the period of crisis and the tensions rising throughout the republic, the move had to be seen as both grossly provocative and even sinister. But the interesting twist was also provided only days later when the Saudi Gazette, which is an English-language weekly, commentated that Mr. Izetbegovic could not automatically count on the unlimited support of the Muslim world without undertaking certain obligations in return, implying that Izetbegovic had, in fact, requested open-ended support of the Muslim world. And that in order to obtain that support he would be expected to undertake certain clear commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, yesterday we discussed the formation and proclamation of Serb Republic of BH on January 9th, 1992. And would you be so kind and share with us, was that a public proclamation pursuant to the Badinter commission which requested the deadline of January 15th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proclamation was a reaction to the imposition of the deadline. As I stated quite frankly yesterday, after the fatal memorandum on sovereign and independent Bosnia-Herzegovina of October 14th, everything done by all sides was both constitutionally and legally dubious. By voting for the memorandum in the absence of Serbian deputies, the SDA/HDZ tactical coalition entered the uncharted waters. And likewise, the Serb plebiscite on November 8th and the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of January 9th were all ad hoc moves in reaction to the perceived attempt by the other two parties to present the Serbs with an unacceptable fait accomplis. In that sense, the announcement by the European Community that January 15th would be the cutoff date for recognition requests had the effect of adding fuel to the fire. It prompted the separatist-minded forces to proceed single-mindedly towards what they regarded as an objective that would be aided and abetted by the international community, while at the same time prompting the Serbs, who would have preferred the status quo, remaining within Yugoslavia, to resort to -- improvised devices that would give expression to their collective will not to be taken into secession. In a funny way, we may compare this situation with that prevailing in Ireland in the run up to the partition of 1921 when both the nationalists and the unionists resorted to a whole host of moves and political and military decisions that were extralegal but reflected their determination not to be forced by the other side into unacceptable solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would ask you something now about the Cutileiro plan, and if you would be so kind and share with us the goals of this plan, the process, and the negotiations which resulted therefrom.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The underlying assumptions of the Cutileiro plan as well as the whole negotiating process initiated by Cutileiro under the auspices of Lord Carrington's negotiating effort were fairly simple. Though assumptions took the pending international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a given and sought to devise the internal rearrangement of the republic along the ethnic lines so as to provide its constituent nations with a sense that they have a stake in the new order of things. To put it very crudely, and I suspect that neither Cutileiro nor Lord Carrington would ever put it as simply as that, but the underlying assumption was that if we are to get the Serbs to agree to Bosnia-Herzegovina's complete secession from Yugoslavia and its internationally recognised independence and sovereignty, let's at least try to devise the internal constitutional rearrangement that would give them the sense of being the masters of their own destiny in the territories where they compromise a majority and removing the very important ingredient in the equation, which was present on all sides, and way was the fear of being dominated and ruled by another ethnicity. Accordingly, the Cutileiro plan proposed the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three ethnically-based cantons, and a central authority in Sarajevo that would have the responsibility for a number of joint functions, including foreign affairs, defence, foreign trade, central bank currency, and so on. And in many ways, it was a mix of federal and confederal ingredients which not only Serbs, but also Croats, found quite attractive. In fact, the leadership of both the Serbian democratic party and the Croatian democratic union was ready and willing to sign on the dotted line and obviously some details concerning the maps that remained to be ironed out. But the ambivalence on the Muslim side was felt even before the referendum on independence, but more strongly in the weeks following it, when Izetbegovic started talking about elements other than ethnic criteria in determining the boundaries of the cantons, such as economic infrastructure or geographic and historical, cultural patterns. When he started mentioning the possibility of more than three cantons, all of which was very alarming to those who believed that it was necessary to provide the blueprint for the constitution rearrangement that would overcome the fear of centralisation among the opponents of full sovereignty and independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the event, after the international recognition of April 6th, 1992, the Muslim side increasingly proved to be disinterested in the continuation of the Cutileiro process, and even though the Karadzic/Boban agreement concluded in Grac, I believe, in the first week of May 1992, left the door open for the SDA to come on board, many commentators believed that with the recognition and with the at least tacit encouragement from Washington to persevere in the demount for a more or less centralised, more or less unitary state, Izetbegovic was no longer interested in the deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it seems to me it is high time to have a short break with your permission. The trial stays adjourned until 5.10. 10 minutes break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, would you be so kind and tell us when Cutileiro plan was actually brought public.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the plan was made public in its main outline in the third week of February. I can't remember the exact date. Certainly, it was in the weeks prior to the referendum of February 29th, March 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please describe the measures taken by the Serbs pursuant to the Cutileiro plan and Badinter commission?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the reaction to the deadline of January 15th, I already indicated was primarily manifested in the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on January 9th. The crisis of the Cutileiro negotiating process manifest in the increasingly unwillingness of Izetbegovic to commit himself to the principle of the tripartite cantonal internal arrangement led to the proclamation of the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on I believe March 28th of 1992. I may be off by one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to bother you, but because of administration of this Tribunal, we have to establish and to spare some time, I will just ask you from the list whether documents 121 from that list, 138, 145, 160, 162, 197, 233, 236, and also 105 and 107 talk about this plan and negotiations regarding these plans.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do indeed. And as far as the reactions of different negotiating parties to the Cutileiro negotiating process are concerned, in some of these articles, suspicion is raised on the Muslim side that prior briefings had been made by the European mediators leading to what they Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. suspected was preconceived outcome vis-a-vis the ethnic tripartite arrangement of the proposed cantons, while on the Serb side, there is an almost oscillating pendulum between encouragement and disappointment, hope and despair, depending on the one hand the vagaries of Izetbegovic's public pronouncements, on the other, continuously optimistic statements by the negotiators and by Cutileiro himself about the prospects for a deal. In retrospect, when we look at these articles, I think that the whole process was doomed by the act of international recognition on April 6th and by the at least implicit encouragement from Washington to Izetbegovic to persevere in his attempt to create a more or less unitary and centralised state, and that the political underpinnings of the Cutileiro assumptions were no longer present after April 6th, which in itself indicates the lack of coherence and diplomatic skill and savoir faire of the international community, because the act of recognition - and I'm now talking about one of those ifs in history - but it's realistic to assume that had the act of recognition been made contingent upon the prior agreement among the parties, such as sought by the Cutileiro plan, then those negotiations could have been crowned with a successful outcome. In view of the fact that recognition was extended not only in the absence of such agreement, but while the negotiating process was fully underway, practically sealed the destiny of the proposed deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion based upon a reasonable degree of certainty whether the measures taken by the Serbs were reasonable and consistent with the Cutileiro plan and Badinter commission?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to answer this question in a value-neutral way that would be divorced from the context of the times. Until the proclamation of the Republika Srpska in July of 1992, all of the statutory and plebiscitary moves by the Serb side could have been fitted in and could have been made compliant with some kind of Bosnia-Herzegovinian wider framework. The plebiscite was a largely symbolic exercise without clear-cut legal consequences. The proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina sought to pre-empt the act of international recognition. The proclamation of constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina sought to emphasise the existence of political and legal structures of the Serb people within Bosnia-Herzegovina that could not be ignored and overcome in the rush for international recognition. But all of them could be made compliant, at least retroactively, with the kind of tripartite internal rearrangement of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was the underlying basis of the Cutileiro plan. Let me be specific: Had the plan been accepted and signed by all three sides, the end result quite possibly would not have been all that different from the end result of Dayton, but the republic would have been spared four and a half years of suffering and bloodshed, and even elementary pragmatism on the side of those who sought separation seems to dictate a modicum of realistic understanding of the impossibility of imposing on one third of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina a dictum that they deemed unacceptable. So what I'm really suggesting in answer to your question is that I cannot judge the reasonableness of those moves from the vantage point of more than a decade later. I would suggest that the way to deal with this judgement, which is obviously a value judgement, is to try and understand the restraints and the metal paradigm and the pressures that were being exerted on the actors at the time, what the French would call l'histoire elementaire, that without putting yourself in the shoes of those people and looking at the options that they were facing and the pressures they're experiencing, simply passing a verdict laden with value connotations such as the reasonableness of their behaviour is very difficult. So I would prefer not to give a clear-cut answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Please share with us your view as academic historian and political scientist how the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For every war, the pivotal question is who fired the first shots. The war between the States, the civil war in the United States, started with the shelling of Fort Sumter in April of 1861. And it was the guns of Fort Sumter that were taken as the clear-cut point. From that point on, it was no longer possible to resolve the problem by political means. The first shots in Bosnia-Herzegovina were fired on March 1st by the Green Berets, the Muslim paramilitary, illegal organisation. And the first victim was a Serb, a man by the name of Nikola Gardovic who was celebrating the wedding of his son. The first mass slaughter of members of one ethnic group by another in Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred in the village of Sijekovac near Bosanski Brod, days later. The victims were Serbs, and the culprits were Muslims and Croats. There is a certain logic to the mindlessness of violence. It is that unfortunately once the shots are fired and lives are lost, the exponential escalation of violence is much more difficult to control. The barricades that started springing up all over the city of Sarajevo in the aftermath of the slaying in Bascarsija on March 1st were admittedly dismantled some days later, and the violence did not completely get out of hand for some weeks to come, but an important threshold had been passed. Unless we bear in mind both the brutalising effect on the mental framework of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina that the war in neighbouring Croatia had had, it will be difficult to understand how was it possible for people who lived in reasonable harmony for a good many decades to succumb to the collective call of the wild and to seek resolution of the conflict by violent means. But it is also important to remember, and this is something that too many people in the international community were not prepared to do, to remember the painful legacy of the relatively recent past still in the living memory of many people, the legacy of 1941 to 1945 which, in the collective memory of the Serbs in both Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, was comparable to the collective memory of the Holocaust among the European Jews. The logic of violence in the months of April and May also reflected different expectations on different sides. As far as the Serbs were concerned, the big uncertainty about the willingness and ability of the YPA to act decisively in order to protect their interests was resolved with its departure and with the leaving of Bosnian-born personnel and a sizable segment of equipment behind. In the case of the HVO, the reliance on Croatian regular units was manifested very early on, particularly in western Herzegovina, and except for the desire to carve out and control an area which was more or less clearly Croat in terms of majority population residing there, in western Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and the Sava River valley, the Croats' essential posture was reactive at this stage rather than proactive. And finally as far as the Muslims were concerned, with the transfer of the paramilitary units into the Territorial Defence and the activation of the pre-existent Patriotic League cells and structures and their blending with the TO in the Muslim-controlled municipalities, we had a numerous, albeit at this stage still, lightly-armed force that was primarily geared to expecting, hoping for, and if necessary provoking foreign intervention by the stunts such as the notorious bread queue massacre in Vase Miskin Street in Sarajevo, and by seeking to expand the territory under its control without entering into an open, all-out military clash of the kind that would display the weaknesses of Muslim-armed formations at that time, all of which is amply documented in the memoirs by Generals Halilovic, Hodzic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And based upon your analysis and literature you reviewed, what was the role of JNA at the beginning of the war and throughout the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important to bear in mind that the JNA developed from the partisan forces during World War II as an explicitly party controlled armed force that sought to identify Yugoslav patriotism with a strictly Titoist form of party political identity and interpretation of history.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: May I interrupt for one moment. Dr. Trifkovic was put forward as an expert historian and not an expert military man. I understand there is going to be an expert called on behalf of the Defence. I'm wondering whether this is properly an area with which he can deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not Trifkovic is not giving an expertise on military matters, but he has to touch upon some military issues because we are talking now about prewar and wartime. And of course, that the war is part of history as well. So I don't think that Mr. Trifkovic will give us a lengthy explanation, but let him tell us a few sentences to be -- because our next questions will be in this context. THE WINTESS: I think that without touching upon strictly military issues -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, please do continue. I don't believe these are strictly military issues. It is more political issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An officer corps nurtured on the legacy of the so-called people's liberation struggle that was the basis of the JNA esprit de corps and the JNA commitment to defending not just Yugoslavia but socialist Yugoslavia based on workers' self-management, nonalignment, brotherhood, unity, and all the rest of it, was a highly politicised view of Yugoslavia, what it meant, what it implied. So with the beginning of disintegration of Yugoslavia, the JNA and its top brass faced a serious problem. On the one hand, part and parcel of their ideological upbringing was that it was impossible for honest, hard-working, good patriotic Yugoslavs to be ethnic separatists, and the refusal to even countenance the possibility of mass ethnic separatism in any ethnic group as part of the JNA doctrine proved well nigh fatal. A nonideological army will postulate different scenarios and different possible threats to the country's stability, sovereignty, and develop different responses to those challenges. In the case of the JNA, we had the utter inability of the top brass to do so because even postulating the possibility of such challenges as were witnessed in Croatia and Slovenia in the summer of 1991 would have been deemed treasonous or politically incorrect. If you're a communist officer in the JNA, and you started talking in 1986, 1987, 1988, or 1989 about the possibility of secession of certain republics and their armed rebellion against the constitutional order, you were putting yourself in a very vulnerable position. And likewise, the insistence of the JNA and of the political party approved of by the JNA which was the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia, their propensity to call all ethnically-based parties in the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina nationalist and to proclaim that they are all equally culpable for the crisis in the republic was perfectly in line with the old Titoist practice of branding all nationalisms together and claiming that they were all equally bad and equally destructive and equally destabilising [Realtime transcript read in error "stabilising"]. So to make the shift and to readjust their mental and political terms of reference to the demand of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have an armed force that would protect their specific right not to be taken into secession by the SDA/HDZ tactical coalition demanded the kind of mental shift that while eminently acceptable for a large number of Bosnian-born Serb lieutenants and majors, and even colonels, certainly when we look at the higher brass of the YPA, the JNA, people such Kadjevic and Hadzic, it becomes obvious this that is the kind of shift that they were simply not able to make, that old Yugo nostalgic assumptions and all ideological mental habits died very hard, and that the rapid developments which they were facing in the second half of 1991 and the first half of 1992 required a qualitatively different kind of response, which in the event was not possible without the emotional commitment that locally-born cadre of the former YPA could have by virtue of being Bosnian Serbs, first and foremost, and former communist party members and YPA officers, next. The same phenomenon, let me add, was at work with many Muslim and Croat officers, except for many of them, the shift was easier to make. Because to a large extent, in both the role of Yugoslavia between the two world wars and in the socialist Yugoslavia after 1945, the Serbs were not only the most prominent propagators of the Yugoslav idea, but also the most committed victims of their own propaganda. And while for a patriotic Slovene, Croat, Bosnian Muslim, or Macedonian, when the old Yugoslav assumptions crumbled away, the new patriotic content was easy to find. For many Serbs, this transformation, this shift proved to be more difficult, more traumatic, and more ambivalent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: May I just make an observation only. It's for the transcript. Can you control, Mr. Lukic, in page 26, line 24, I think Dr. Trifkovic said "destablising," and it says here "equally stabilising." Can you confirm what you say, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is destablising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Destablising. Please correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, staying in the context, describe for us, please, the actions taken by the Muslims, Bosnian Muslims, with respect to forming their own army, EA, Patriotic League, Green Berets, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret not having at my disposal some of the memoirs of the early Muslim activists who were instrumental in developing and setting up both the Patriotic League and the Green Beret units which came into my possession subsequent to my preparation of the report. But the story is verified by the fact that from different sources, different direct participants in these events, provide a similar timetable. The pivotal point in March 31st, 1991, four months before the crisis in Croatia and Slovenia when the SDA activists meeting in a mosque at Souk Bunar near Sarajevo decided to set up a rudimentary network of local activists who would be charged with preparing and developing a party militia which they would call Patriotic League. The early efforts received their full imprimatur on June 10th, 1991 - let me emphasise, still two weeks before the violence started with the Slovene and Croatian declaration of independence - with the meeting of leading Muslim intellectuals and SDA activists attended by Alija Izetbegovic himself, at which detailed instructions were prepared for field activists and the overall territorial principle of these efforts was accepted as suggested by I believe it was Halilovic himself who said that instead of going after a small body of highly-trained experts in the militia and command sabotage, they ought to seek a broadly-based mass movement that would have its outposts in more or less every municipality of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Highly significant is the fact that at that meeting it was decided to set up nine regional staffs of the Patriotic League of which one was outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, in southwest Serbia, the area that the Muslims call Sandjak. And in subsequent testimonies and statements by the authors of different memoirs and serialised articles in Oslobodenje and Darne and elsewhere, several of these Muslim activists readily concede that they were hoping that if and when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they would be helped by an uprising of the Muslims in Sandjak and the Albanians in Kosovo, and that furthermore they were disappointed that this would not happen in the spring and summer of 1992. By the 2nd of December of 1991, when a detailed military council, again attended by Izetbegovic, was held in a private house on the outskirts of Sarajevo, the Patriotic League had branches in 104 of 107 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and two months later, when a further military council was held in the village of Mahurici, near Travnik, where a whole series of specific instructions concerning the future developments were issued, by that time, we are looking at a fairly strong and centralised force of close to a hundred thousand men, which while devoid of heavy weaponry, had a detailed command and control structure and compartmentalisation into different arms and services resembling the fully fledged armed force which, as I mentioned earlier, only two months later was indeed blended into the TO which then was turned into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the initial impetus came on 31st of March of 1991. The detailed blueprint was elaborated on June 10th of 1991. The review of the fruits was summarised in -- on December 2nd of 1991. And the elaboration of specific tasks in the anticipated violence ahead was considered in some detail at Mahurici in the second half of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this whole preparation by the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina done before the referendum held in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was it done before the referendum, but the military council at Mahurici which the Muslims themselves called historic in their own literature was specifically convened in order to consider the state of military preparedness for the aftermath of the referendum. Because they had no doubt that the referendum was the kind of challenge to the Serbs to which they were expected to react in more than merely political way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Prior to April 1992, was there the declaration of imminent threat of war, and when was the state of imminent threat of war declared, and by whom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date without consulting my papers, but it was proclaimed before the international recognition. I believe -- I'm sorry, I'm not able to answer it offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the literature you reviewed, did you have the opportunity to familiarise yourself with the role of the police during the state of imminent threat of war with respect to the military?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I'm sorry. I haven't objected so far, but none of this, what we're now dealing with, is, in fact, in the report. I think if Dr. Trifkovic is now going to start dealing with the role of the police, then I would like to know on what literature he's relying, on what documents he's relying, not just a general assertion in this way I'm afraid. There are a number of other matters I would be asking for references for, but I don't want to detain the doctor any further. But on this, I would like to know on what he is going to refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, are you familiar with the law of all people's defence and self-protection?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with its broad outline including the summary of the law that is also widely available in English. It is a cumbersome document in the original which I readily admit to not having read in its entirety in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you, based on your knowledge, answer my previous question, if you know what is prescribed in this law about the role of police?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the simple answer -- I have no objection if Mr. Lukic wants to put the law in. Rather than having a guess or a memory of what's in this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I would prefer to give fairly specific answers to matters I am fully familiar with, I would prefer not to deal with issues where I'm not as briefed as I like to be when providing an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Again, because of the procedural matters, I'll just ask you whether the documents listed on this table are based for your conclusions regarding the war. And those documents are 001, 002, 003, 006, 115, 216, and 224.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they refer to what I mentioned earlier as a whole series of memoirs and personal accounts and reminiscences by various Bosnian Muslim activists and commanders who are surprisingly frank and forthright in their accounts of their preparations, military preparations, even in the period when the public face of the SDA was full of statements about peaceful intentions and determination to resolve all problems by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like you -- I would like to ask you, based upon your review of the documents provided, meaning Donia's report, numerous articles and literature, among other things, please describe Dr. Stakic's role before the takeover of Prijedor Municipality on April 30th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think it's interesting that Dr. Stakic is a relative latecomer to the ranks of the SDS. In the early days of the multiparty renaissance in the former Yugoslavia, he joined the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic, a political organisation that was initiated by a Belgrade-based lawyer by the name of Veljko Guberina, I believe, in 1989, which followed in the footsteps of the well-known Serbian politician from the late 19th and early 20th century who I must emphasise followed the path of social radicalism, which is whence the party got its name. It should not be confused with the later product of the Yugoslav political imbroglio, the Serbian radical party of Vojislav Seselj. Following in Pasic's tradition meant social justice of a distinctly leftish kind when it came to issues of income distribution, land reform, provision of public services. And the desire to give expression to ethnic particularism within the Yugoslav framework. And I emphasise not only that that would give expression to the Serb particularism but also other groups. Because let us not forget that as one of the early prime ministers of Yugoslavia or the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes as it was known then, Nikola Pasic relentlessly worked on the reconciliation with the Croats the work which was crowned with the successful conclusion of the coalition between his radicals and Stipe Radic's Croatian peasant party in 1925. Also, I must say that reading some of Dr. Stakic's speeches and statements from 1991, I was struck by the difference in tone between his approach and that of people clearly identified with the renaissance of Serbian national idea, at that time people like Vuk Draskovic, for instance. Most notably, I believe that his address at the celebration of the republic day in Prijedor on November 29th, 1991, was such an extravagant ode to the Yugoslav idea and to the spirit of Yugoslavism and Yugoslav togetherness, that in itself it would have sounded pretty suspicious, if not outright odious, to a genuine Serb nationalist at the time because by that time, explicit nationalists were no longer talking in terms of preserving Yugoslavia, but of re-inventing a Serb entity that would seek to unite all Serbs on the ruins of Yugoslavia. So as late as the end of 1991, in his public statements, Dr. Stakic reflected the mindset of what I would colloquially call "Yugo nostalgia," the hope for the revival of the old Yugoslav spirit of togetherness, even though by that time, to a political realist, it would have been increasingly obvious that the exercise was forlorn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, excuse me. We have run out of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am also running out of voice. So thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So it's in our mutual interest to finish these hearings today. I would like to thank you, all participants, for your cooperation. And for you, Dr. Trifkovic, I would like to remind you that until your testimony here has concluded, you may not contact representatives either the Defence or the Prosecution. Please be back on Monday at 9.00 a.m. to continue with the evidence in this case. The trial stays adjourned until Monday at 9.00 a.m. in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just think that Dr. Trifkovic in light of the fact that he's still in chief shouldn't think he'll be leaving here on Monday because I don't think he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: at 6.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 17th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
